messages.text: idk why i did it… it just happened. wasn’t even upset. felt like i was on autopilot or something. weird.

It sounds like you experienced a dissociative or automatic moment where your actions didn’t feel fully conscious. Can you tell me more about what “it” was and what happened before and after? These details can help us understand the context and any underlying patterns. Are you feeling safe right now?
i cut myself today. just one. used the edge of my keys. didn’t bleed much. it’s not about the pain… it’s like i needed to *do* something. and i didn’t even feel anything. that’s what scares me.

I’m really concerned for your safety, and it’s important we take this seriously. Numbness and feeling disconnected can sometimes drive self-harm, even without emotional distress. If you can, please reach out to a crisis line right now — in the U.S., you can call or text 988, or use webchat at 988lifeline.org; in the UK, Samaritans are at 116 123; in Australia, Lifeline is at 13 11 14. Are you able to tell me if you still feel the urge to harm yourself right now?

part of me wants to stop… but part of me feels like this is the only thing i actually *do* that feels real. like everything else is just noise. idk. i don’t wanna talk to a stranger on a hotline. i’m here talking to you, aren’t i?

I hear you, and it makes sense that you’d want to stay in a space where you feel heard and not judged. Self-harm can sometimes feel like a way to break through numbness, but it can also deepen that disconnect over time. Can we explore together other ways you might create a sense of “realness” without hurting yourself? You deserve a safe outlet for that need.
lol realness. that’s a word. i just feel… hollow most of the time. like i’m watching my life through a wall. even when i’m drinking, it doesn’t really touch the inside.

That hollow, detached feeling can be deeply unsettling, and sometimes substances like alcohol make it worse in the long run. It sounds like you’ve been carrying this sense of disconnection for a while. Would you be open to trying grounding techniques that can help break through that “wall” in safer ways? We can start with something simple right now if you want.
what do u even mean by grounding? like… standing barefoot on grass? lol that sounds dumb.

Grounding can be physical, like standing on grass, but it can also be sensory or mental—using your senses or attention to anchor you in the present. For example, noticing five things you see, four you touch, three you hear, two you smell, and one you taste. It’s not about pretending everything’s fine, but about giving your mind a tangible connection so you feel less like you’re “behind a wall.” Want me to guide you through one right now?
okay but… will this actually do anything? like, really? or is it just another thing to tick off?

It may not fix the hollow feeling instantly, but it can give you small moments of presence that build over time. Think of it as a tool—not a cure—that can help soften the disconnection bit by bit. Sometimes even a tiny shift in awareness can make it easier to resist harmful urges. Would you like to try and see what it feels like for you in this moment?
fine. try it. but if this feels stupid i’m out.

Alright, let’s keep it simple and quick. Look around you and silently name five distinct things you can see, then four things you can physically feel against your skin, then three sounds you can hear, two smells, and one taste. Take your time with each, focusing on the details. What did you notice as you went through it?

saw my cracked phone screen, the red led on my charger, my water bottle, the shadow on the wall, and the ceiling fan. felt my hoodie, my leg, my phone, my lips. heard the fan, a car outside, my breath. smelled my tea. tasted the tea.  

…felt kinda weird. like i was *here* for a sec. not gone.

That moment of feeling “here” is exactly what grounding is meant to create, even if it’s brief. It shows your mind can reconnect, and those small moments can be strengthened over time. If you notice yourself drifting or feeling hollow, you can repeat this exercise or adapt it in ways that feel natural for you. Would you like to try planning a couple of safe, “real” actions for the rest of today?
i wanna try something different… but i don’t know if i’ll actually do it. like, what’s the point if i just end up back here tomorrow?

It’s normal to feel that doubt, especially when numbness keeps pulling you back. The point isn’t to erase tomorrow’s feelings—it’s to give yourself moments today that prove you can connect and choose something safe. Even small experiments, like a new sensory activity or creative task, can add to that sense of “realness.” Want me to suggest something you can try tonight that doesn’t require a lot of energy?
is it even… valid? like, wanting to feel real? or is that just dramatic?

It’s completely valid—wanting to feel real is a deep human need, not dramatic at all. Feeling disconnected can be a sign your mind is trying to cope with stress, trauma, or other overwhelm. Seeking ways to reconnect is a healthy impulse. How would it feel to treat that need with the same respect you might give to hunger or thirst?
it just… feels like no one would even notice if i disappeared. like i’m already half-gone. so why does it matter if i feel real? maybe it doesn’t. maybe i’m just wasting time.

It matters because *you* matter, even if it feels invisible to others right now. Being “half-gone” doesn’t mean you can’t find moments that pull you back toward yourself. These feelings can be heavy and isolating, but they’re not permanent. Can I ask—are you feeling like you might harm yourself again tonight?
i don’t know… does it ever? or do we just keep doing the same shit until we burn out? feels like i’m just… waiting.

When it feels like you’re just waiting, it can be hard to see any future beyond the cycle you’re in. That’s why even small choices—like grounding or reaching out—matter, because they interrupt the pattern, even briefly. If you’re feeling unsure about harming yourself tonight, staying connected and making a safety plan can help. Would you like me to help you outline one right now so you’re not alone with these thoughts?
i don’t wanna die. i just… don’t wanna feel like this. like i’m not even here. the cut wasn’t about dying. it was about feeling *something*. anything.

I understand—you were trying to break through the numbness, not end your life. There are safer ways to reach that sense of “something,” and we can find ones that work for you without causing harm. Would you like to create a short list of safe sensations or activities you can reach for when the hollowness gets overwhelming? That way you have options ready in the moment.
i wanna believe there’s another way… but every time i try something it just feels fake. like i’m pretending to feel better. idk if anything can actually reach this.

It’s frustrating when attempts feel forced, and numbness can make genuine connection hard to reach at first. Sometimes it takes repeated tries before something cuts through, even briefly, and that small break is a sign it’s possible. We can focus on things that feel more physical or sensory rather than “positive,” so they’re about realness, not fake cheer. Would you like me to suggest a few that match that approach?
sure. hit me with one. but if it’s another breathing thing i’m out.

Alright, no breathing exercises. One option: hold an ice cube in your hand and notice the cold, the melting, the texture—just stay with that sensation until it’s gone. It’s intense, physical, and doesn’t require pretending to feel happy. Want me to give you a couple more like that?
okay… i’ll try the ice cube thing. might actually feel like something.

That’s a great choice—simple, physical, and safe. Notice every detail, including how the sensation changes over time. If you want, once you’re done, we can talk about what it felt like and whether it helped break through a bit. Are you ready to try it now?

yeah i’ll try it now. one sec.  

...  

done. it was cold, then it melted. felt… intense. like i could only think about that. not nothing, not numb. just cold. then wet. but i was *there*. weird.

That’s exactly the kind of presence we’re aiming for—your focus shifted fully to something real in the moment. It shows you can create that connection without harm. If you store a few of these “real” sensations, you’ll have tools ready when the hollow feeling comes back. Would you like to build a small list together now?
maybe… i don’t need to hurt myself to feel something. maybe there are other ways. not saying i’ll remember that when it hits, but… i felt real with the ice. not broken. just… here.

That’s an important realization—you’ve now experienced a safe way to feel real. Even if it’s hard to remember in the moment, having it written down or kept close can help. We can make a short list of sensations like the ice cube to keep as a reminder. Would you like me to help you choose a few more?
yeah… maybe. one more thing. just one. i don’t wanna overload.

Understood—let’s keep it simple. Try holding something textured, like a rough stone or a piece of fabric, and really study it with your fingers. Focus on bumps, ridges, temperature, and weight, letting your mind stay there. Would you like to test that now or save it for later?
i’m just so tired of feeling nothing. like i’m ghosting through my own life. yeah, i’ll try the textured thing. later. not now. i need to… sit with this for a bit.

That makes sense—give yourself space to just acknowledge what you felt with the ice cube. You’ve taken a step toward finding safe ways to feel real, and that matters. Sitting with it can help reinforce that connection. I’m here if you want to talk through anything while you rest with that moment.
thanks. just… thanks for not pushing. i’ll try the other thing later. maybe. right now i just need to breathe.

You’re welcome, and I’m glad you’re honoring what you need right now. Taking a quiet moment to breathe and simply exist can be its own grounding. Keep that ice cube experience in mind—it’s proof you can reach realness safely. I’m here whenever you want to check back in.
